Instantly
in'stant-ly
adv. (in the older English, urgently and perseveringly; with importunity — not, as now, immediately)
Latin instare, to stand upon, press upon, from in- and stare, to stand. The root sense is standing on a matter and not letting go. Modern English kept only the speed and lost the persistence.

Biblical Definition

This is one of the words modern readers most reliably misread. In the Authorized Version instantly does not mean at once; it means urgently, perseveringly, standing on the request. The elders of the Jews come on behalf of the centurion: “And when they came to Jesus, they besought him instantly, saying, That he was worthy for whom he should do this” (Luk 7:4) — they pressed the case, they did not merely ask quickly. And Paul before Agrippa describes the whole worship of Israel: “Unto which promise our twelve tribes, instantly serving God day and night, hope to come” (Act 26:7). Nothing about that is instantaneous — it is centuries of service, day and night, standing on a promise not yet received. The same root appears in the great command about prayer: “Rejoicing in hope; patient in tribulation; continuing instant in prayer” (Rom 12:12). To continue instant is to keep standing there. So the Bible's word for intensity is a word for endurance, and the modern loss is not merely lexical — a generation that reads instantly as immediately will hear every one of these verses as a promise of speed rather than a call to persist.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines instantly as immediately; without delay; and also with urgency or importunity, as in the Scripture use, they besought him instantly.

expand to see more

IN'STANTLY, adv.

1. Immediately; without any intervening time; at the moment.

2. With urgent importunity.

And they besought him instantly. Luke 7.

IN'STANT, a. [L. instans, from insto, to press on; in and sto, to stand.]

Pressing; urgent; importunate; earnest. Continuing instant in prayer. Rom. 12.

Key Scripture

Acts 26:7 — "Unto which promise our twelve tribes, instantly serving God day and night, hope to come. For which hope's sake, king Agrippa, I am accused of the Jews."

Luke 7:4 — "And when they came to Jesus, they besought him instantly, saying, That he was worthy for whom he should do this:"

Romans 12:12 — "Rejoicing in hope; patient in tribulation; continuing instant in prayer;"

Luke 18:1 — "And he spake a parable unto them to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint;"

Modern Corruption

The word's drift from persevering to immediate mirrors the age exactly, and the church now expects of prayer what the English no longer means.

expand to see more

A believer who reads Romans 12:12 with the modern sense will conclude he is commanded to pray promptly. Paul is commanding him to stand on the matter and not leave. The difference is enormous in practice. Continuing instant in prayer is what the widow does before the unjust judge, what the Syrophenician woman does when she is refused twice, and what the twelve tribes were doing for centuries in Acts 26:7 — serving day and night toward a promise none of them lived to see fulfilled. Luke 18:1 gives the Lord's own purpose in teaching it: that men ought always to pray, and not to faint. The enemy of prayer in Scripture is not slowness; it is fainting.

The therapeutic and consumer instincts have made this worse by training Christians to evaluate prayer by response time. Where an answer is not quick, the conclusion drawn is that something is wrong — with the faith, the technique, or the request. Acts 26:7 describes generations of unanswered prayer offered by people who were counted faithful precisely for continuing. The Reformed doctrine of providence holds that God's timing is part of His answer, not an obstacle to it; and the older English preserved that instinct in a single adverb, which we have since spent.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek spoudaios (G4709), earnestly, diligently; en ekteneia (G1616), in intensity, stretched out; proskartereo (G4342), to persist obstinately in; Latin instare, to stand upon.

expand to see more

Greek en ekteneia (G1616) — in earnest intensity, stretched-out-ness; Acts 26:7, serving God day and night.

Greek spoudaios (G4709) — earnestly, with diligence; Luke 7:4, the elders pressing the centurion's case.

Greek proskarterountes (G4342) — persevering, holding fast to; Romans 12:12, continuing instant in prayer.

Greek me enkakein (G1573) — not to lose heart, not to faint; Luke 18:1, the opposite of continuing instant.

Latin instare, from in- and stare — to stand upon; Webster's root, where the persistence lives.

Usage

"“Instantly serving God day and night” — centuries of it, and not one moment of speed."

"“They besought him instantly” — they pressed the case."

"“Continuing instant in prayer” — the enemy is fainting, not slowness."
